Owner decision, 17 Nov 2026: 'Ok let's lower the bar.' Thrum is a game engine; the aim is the most plausible result as fast as possible, not physical accuracy. New bar for rendering and visual work: it looks as good as shipped high-end games, judged against an agent-written visual inspection list, and it runs fast, with performance as tripwires (no invented budgets). Physical or f64 references stop being pass/fail gates: they stay as diagnostic tools used when output looks wrong, to find the cause. Exact image baselines stay only where they guard against unintended regressions, not to block deliberate shader changes. Correctness proofs stay where failures are silent and costly: networking and transport, simulation determinism, asset and cooked formats, contracts between modules. Also make proof proportional to risk: small fix rounds and tripwire records shouldn't get the same review weight as new rendering work, and cut evidence items that cost more than the risk they cover. Apply this to ORCHESTRATE.md, the thrum-engineering skill (.agents/skills/thrum-engineering), docs/design/AI-DEVELOPMENT.md and AI-PERFORMANCE.md where they set the bar, and every open module's DESIGN, PLAN and DONE.json for milestones not yet Done (CLOUDS's M3 two-stream model, ATMOSPHERE, WATERS, APPLE-PRESENTATION and so on): rewrite or drop items that gate on accuracy rather than look and speed. Milestones currently being built or Ready for Review keep their items unless an item is now clearly pointless; say which you changed in flight. Record the owner's decision and date where the settings record decisions. Don't change modules' scope or the V1 exit beyond the bar. Done when the settings, skill, design docs and done-when files say the new bar consistently, ./dev check-docs passes, and your report lists each module's dropped or rewritten items and an estimate of reviews and fix rounds saved.

Builders are blocking on the "no exact baseline moves" item. About 60 open items across 18 modules (CLOUDS WP7.9, RAY-TRACING WP4.10, SESSION WP5.10, WATERS WP13.13, RENDER-2D WP3.11 and WP3.13, GAME-SPLIT, GAME-UI, PUDDLES, RIVERS, SWARM, SHOWCASE and others) check with `python3 scripts/exact_baselines.py verify`, which without --full delegates to `agent_loop.py main-check exact-images`; orchestrate refuses any item check that invokes main-check, so each of those work packages blocks (CLOUDS WP7 and RAY-TRACING WP4 have, and REPO-RULES WP5 already had its copy removed). Fix this once for the whole project rather than per module.

The lead's assumption, which the owner can overturn: the registered main-branch check `exact-images` (ORCHESTRATE.md) already guards that no baseline moves after every merge, and the owner wants fast merges with long proofs on main, not in each work package. So remove these items where nothing else in the work package depends on them, or replace them with something the work package can show before the merge, such as a check that it changed no registered baseline or comparison file. Do not make each work package run `verify --full`. Change scripts/exact_baselines.py in its owning module only if that is the cleaner fix. Put CLOUDS WP7 and RAY-TRACING WP4 first, since their builders have finished and wait only on this.

The main-branch check cross-target (bash scripts/check_cross_target.sh) fails on main; last pass 84d1e63db, failing since about 1eab8c000, and the script couldn't tell which commit broke it. Diagnosis from the lead: the x86_64-pc-windows-msvc check fails with error[E0432] at crates/thrum-render/tests/ray_structure_lifecycle_gpu.rs:7, unresolved import super::ray_support. The file declares `pub mod ray_support` under #[cfg(all(target_os = "macos", feature = "creation-counters"))] but `mod metal` and its `use super::ray_support::support` only under #[cfg(feature = "creation-counters")], so any non-macOS build with creation-counters on fails. The file itself is old, so something between those commits probably started building it with that feature for Windows (GAME-SPLIT WP3's feature changes and RAY-TRACING WP4 both landed then). Find the cause, then plan the smallest fix in the owning module as its next work package or a plan change, so cross-target passes again. Also check whether other test files share the same cfg mismatch.
